items.title: 9.2 Real Life Applications of Remainder and Factor Theorems

blocks.text: In this article, we will demonstrate how remainder and factor theorems are applied in different areas such as polynomial regression (used in statistical modeling), signal processing (used for filtering and error detection) and coding theory (used in data encryption and error correction in communication systems). These applications highlight the significance of polynomial analysis beyond theoretical mathematics.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
All three applications use the same two facts from 9.1.1 and 9.1.2:
1. Remainder theorem: the value \(P(a)\) is the remainder on dividing \(P(x)\) by \(x - a\), so evaluating a model at an input is the same as finding a remainder.
2. Factor theorem: \(P(a) = 0\) exactly when \(x - a\) is a factor, i.e. \(a\) is a root.
In the examples below, "predicted value" or "system response" simply means \(P(a)\).

It is a type of regression analysis where the relationship between the independent and dependent variables is modeled as an \(n^{\text{th}}\)-degree polynomial. It is used when the data shows a curved (non-linear) relationship, but we still want to fit a smooth, continuous function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In simple words: we have data (for example sales in each month) and we choose a polynomial \(P(x)\) whose graph passes close to the data points. Then \(P(x)\) is the predicted (model) value at \(x\), and
\[\text{Error} = \text{Observed} - \text{Predicted}\]
A small error means the model fits well at that point.

blocks.title: Example 8
blocks.problem: Consider a data set of monthly sales figures. A polynomial regression model \(P(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} + 2x + 1\) is fitted to this data. If the observed sales in the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) month are 40 units, find the percentage error.
steps:
Given: \(P(x) = x^{3} + x^{2} + 2x + 1\); observed sales in month 3 \(= 40\) units.
To find: the percentage error at \(x = 3\).
Method: the predicted value is \(P(3)\), which by the remainder theorem is the remainder on dividing \(P(x)\) by \(x - 3\). Then Error = Observed − Predicted, and the percentage error compares the size of the error with the observed value.

Step 1: Predicted sales
\[P(3) = 3^{3} + 3^{2} + 2(3) + 1\]
\[= 27 + 9 + 6 + 1 = 43\]
Why: the model's prediction for month 3 is its value at \(x = 3\).

Step 2: Error
\[\text{Error} = 40 - P(3) = 40 - 43 = -3\]
Why: Error = Observed − Predicted. The negative sign means the model predicted 3 units more than were actually sold.

Step 3: Percentage error
\[\left|\dfrac{-3}{40}\right| \times 100 = 7.5\%\]
Why: the book divides the size of the error (absolute value, so no sign) by the observed value and multiplies by 100.

Check:
\(7.5\%\) of 40 is \(0.075 \times 40 = 3\), the size of the error.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: A quadratic regression model is \(P(x) = x^{2} + ax + 12\). If regression model fitted accurately at \(x = -3\), then find the value of \(a\).
steps:
Given: \(P(x) = x^{2} + ax + 12\), fitted accurately at \(x = -3\).
To find: \(a\).
Method: the book reads "fitted accurately at \(x = -3\)" as "\(x = -3\) is a root", so \(P(-3) = 0\). By the factor theorem this also means \(x + 3\) is a factor.

blocks.text: It is used in computers or digital devices to analyze, change or improve signals like sound, images or sensor data. The remainder theorem is a powerful mathematical tool in DSP that simplifies the evaluation of system responses, stability checks and frequency analysis. If the remainder is zero, it means that the system has no error at that input.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: A digital signal processing system is represented by the polynomial \(P(z) = z^{4} - 3z^{3} + 2z^{2} + z - 5\). Find the system response at \(z = -1\) using the remainder theorem.
steps:
Given: \(P(z) = z^{4} - 3z^{3} + 2z^{2} + z - 5\).
To find: the system response at \(z = -1\).
Method: by the remainder theorem the response \(P(-1)\) is the remainder on dividing \(P(z)\) by \(z + 1\). If it is zero, the system has no error at that input.

Step 1: Evaluate each term at \(z = -1\)
\[(-1)^{4} = 1,\quad -3(-1)^{3} = 3\]
\[2(-1)^{2} = 2,\quad (-1) = -1\]
Why: even powers of \(-1\) are 1 and odd powers are \(-1\); evaluating term by term avoids sign mistakes.

Step 2: Add the terms
\[\text{Remainder} = P(-1)\]
\[= 1 + 3 + 2 - 1 - 5 = 0\]
Why: the constant \(-5\) is added unchanged.

Step 3: Interpret
Since \(P(-1) = 0\), the system has no error at \(z = -1\).
Why: the book's rule for DSP: remainder zero means no error at that input. By the factor theorem, \(z + 1\) is also a factor of \(P(z)\).

Check by synthetic division (\(a = -1\)):
\[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} -1 & 1 & -3 & 2 & 1 & -5 \\ & & -1 & 4 & -6 & 5 \\ \hline & 1 & -4 & 6 & -5 & \boxed{0} \end{array}\]
The remainder is 0, as found.
blocks.answer: \(P(-1) = 0\): the system response at \(z = -1\) is 0, so the system has no error at \(z = -1\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The predicted value or system response at an input \(a\) is \(P(a)\), which is the remainder on dividing by \(x - a\).
2. Error = Observed − Predicted; percentage error (as in the book) \(= \left|\frac{\text{Error}}{\text{Observed}}\right| \times 100\).
3. "Fitted accurately at \(a\)" (Example 9) and "no error at \(a\)" (Example 10) are both used in the book to mean \(P(a) = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Writing Error = Predicted − Observed; the book uses Observed − Predicted.
2. Keeping the minus sign in a percentage error; take the absolute value.
3. Sign slips with \(-3(-1)^{3}\): it is \(+3\), not \(-3\).
